Why Squishy Toys?

Before we dive into the comparison, let's talk about why squishy toys have become such a massive category. These soft, squeezable little critters aren't just cute desk decorations — they're legitimate tools for sensory regulation, stress relief, and fine motor skill development.

Teachers use them as classroom prize box rewards. Occupational therapists recommend them for kids with sensory processing needs. Parents stock them for party favor bags and goodie bags. And let's be honest — even adults love having a satisfying squish within arm's reach at their desk.

The real question is: when you're buying in bulk, should you go for the smaller, more curated set or the massive value pack? Let's break it down.

What We Loved About the 30 Pack Squishy Toys

The first thing you notice when you open the 30 Pack Squishy Toys is the packaging. It comes in a colorful, sturdy gift box that immediately says "this is a real present" — not "here's a bag of stuff." For something you're giving to a child as a gift or using as a classroom prize, that presentation matters a lot.

Every single squishy is individually wrapped. That means you don't have to sort, bag, or store them differently — they're already portioned out and ready to hand over. For a teacher stocking a prize box or a parent assembling party favor bags, this is a huge time saver. You can literally grab and go.

The size range (1 to 2 inches) means you get some squishies that are substantial enough to feel satisfying and some that are tiny and cute. The styles are random, which adds an element of surprise — our test kids loved the "mystery box" feel of not knowing which animal or fruit they'd pull out.

The material is soft and non-toxic, made from TPR that passes child safety standards. It doesn't have that plasticky chemical smell some cheap toys have, and the squishies spring back to shape even after aggressive squeezing. One of our testers (a particularly enthusiastic 6-year-old) confirmed they're "super squishable" — high praise from the target demographic.

We also appreciated that they're washable. Kids' toys get grimy fast, and being able to rinse these off with warm water and let them air dry is a practical win that parents will notice.

Where the 100 Pack Shines

The 100 Pack Mochi Squishy Toys is the quantity champion here, and there's no denying the math: $16.99 for 100 squishies comes out to about $0.17 per toy. That's a screaming deal if you need a lot of them.

If you're stuffing a piñata, filling Easter eggs, or prepping for a classroom carnival where you're going through prizes by the handful, the 100 Pack is the practical choice. The shapes include a fun mix of animals (cats, dogs, bunnies, bears) and food items (donuts, hamburgers, sushi, ice cream) that cover the popular kawaii aesthetic. For sensory play, the slow-rise squish provides a calming, tactile experience that's especially beneficial for kids who need regulation tools.

Durability & Longevity

We tested both sets over two weeks with a panel of kids ages 3–12 (yes, we have the best job). Key findings:

30 Pack Squishy Toys: The slightly larger size (some hitting 2 inches) means thicker material that holds up well to repeated squishing. After 14 days of active play, we saw no tears or permanent deformation. The colors stayed bright, and a quick wash with warm water removed dirt and hand oils completely.

100 Pack Mochi Squishies: The smaller, thinner construction is more prone to tearing if handled roughly — particularly the more detailed shapes with thin sections (like animal legs or food details). That said, for typical gentle squishing and fidget use, they held up fine. The material's slow-rise quality is genuinely satisfying, and many of our adult testers preferred the feel of the mochi texture.

Pro Tip: Both sets use similar non-toxic TPR/silicone blend materials. The main durability difference comes from the size — larger = thicker walls = tougher. If your kids tend to be rough, the 30 Pack's larger average size gives it an edge.

Sensory & Therapeutic Value

Both products excel in the sensory toy category, and for good reason. Squishy toys provide proprioceptive input — the sensory feedback from resistance and pressure — that helps regulate the nervous system. That's not marketing fluff; it's based on established occupational therapy principles.

For kids (and adults) with anxiety, ADHD, autism, or sensory processing differences, having a small, discreet fidget toy can be genuinely grounding. The 30 Pack's individually wrapped squishies are easy to keep in a desk drawer or backpack, ready to deploy when focus or calm is needed.

Teachers told us they prefer having a stash of individually wrapped squishies because they can hand one out without any prep — and because kids value the "treasure" experience of unwrapping something new. The 100 Pack, while more economical, lacks that instant-gratification factor.
